blocks.text: On the hen's love for her chicks.

It remains for us to say something about the hen's love for her chicks, in connection with the notable passage of Christ, Matth. XXIII, 37. and Luc. XIII, 34.: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!" Hen in Greek is ὄρνις [ornis], a word which among the older Greeks signified bird in general. Yet in Plato, Laws book 7, ὀρνίθων θρέμματα [ornithōn thremmata] are thought to be the chicks of hens. And in Aristophanes, in the Wasps, ὀρνίθων γάλα [ornithōn gala] is hens' milk. And in Aristotle οἱ ὄρνιθες [hoi ornithes] are cocks, when he writes in Hist. book 9, ch. 50: Ἐκτέμνονται δὲ οἱ ὄρνιθες κατὰ τὸ ὀῤῥοπύγιον [ektemnontai de hoi ornithes kata to orrhopygion], that is, Cocks are castrated near the rump. And αἱ ὄρνιθες [hai ornithes] are hens in De generat. anim. book 1, ch. 21, where he reports that some people περὶ τὰς ὄρνιθας τὰς γενναίας σπουδάζειν [peri tas ornithas tas gennaias spoudazein], take pains to breed well-bred hens. Nor is anything else meant in these words of Theophrastus, De causis book 2, ch. 15: Τὰ ὅλως εὔτοκα βραχύβια· καὶ τὰ ὑπερτοκήσαντα πολλάκις ἀπόλλυται, καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν τε συνανθρωπευομένων αἱ ὄρνιθες [ta holōs eutoka brachybia; kai ta hypertokēsanta pollakis apollytai, kai malista epi tōn te synanthrōpeuomenōn hai ornithes]. This should certainly be rendered thus: All the most prolific animals are short-lived; and those whose breeding is excessive often perish, and hens above all among those that live with humans. Nor in these words of Chrysippus in Athenaeus, book 9, ch. 4: Καθάπερ τινὲς τὰς λευκὰς ὀρνίθας τῶν μελανῶν ἡδίους εἶναι μᾶλλον [kathaper tines tas leukas ornithas tōn melanōn hēdious einai mallon]; As some hold that white hens are tastier than black ones. And he likewise proves, by adducing examples, that the old comic poets Menander, Cratinus and Antiphanes used it for hens. And in the same author, book 1, ch. 15, Phylarchus relates that τινὰς δυνάμεις στυτικὰς [tinas dynameis stytikas] sent by Sandrocottus, king of the Indians, to Seleucus, ὁρμὰς ἐμποιεῖν ὀρνίθων δίκην [hormas empoiein ornithōn dikēn], excited sexual desire, such as is found in cocks. A very great man noted on that passage that στυπτικὰς [styptikas] is wrongly printed; and that the translator substituted Sandropyctus for Sandrocottus, Antiochus for Seleucus, and little sparrows for cocks, so that nothing sound remains in this passage. Since, then, ὄρνις [ornis] in Homer and Hesiod is nothing other than bird in general, in Plato's age it began to be used for the gallinaceous kind, and for some centuries was said of the cock as well as of the hen, until usage prevailed that it was the proper name of the hen. Hence Myrtilus in Athenaeus, book 9: Ἀλλὰ [II, 696] μὴν καὶ ὄρνιθας καὶ ὀρνίθια νῦν μόνον ἡ συνήθεια καλεῖ τὰς θηλείας [alla mēn kai ornithas kai ornithia nyn monon hē synētheia kalei tas thēleias]; Now indeed custom has it that only the females (of cocks) are called ὄρνιθες [ornithes] and ὀρνίθια [ornithia]. Therefore in Matthew and Luke ὄρνις [ornis] is not طير [ṭayr] or طاير [ṭāyir], bird in general, as the Vulgate translator renders it in Luke, and as one of the Arabic versions renders it in Luke and the other in both places, but دجاجة [dajāja], hen, as the Vulgate translator and Erpenianus have it in Matthew. Accordingly the Syriac too consistently renders ܬܪܢܓܘܠܬܐ, and the Ethiopic ዶርሆ፡, that is, hen. So also Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, and most of the ancients, except Ambrose on Luke, where this passage is rendered thus: How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird its nest under its feathers? But this is most especially proper to the hen, that she not only sits on her eggs, like the other birds, but also gathers her chicks, once hatched, under her wings, so that they may be warmed and invigorated [col. 126] by their mother's heat. Hence it is that in Arabic she is surnamed ام حفصة [umm ḥafṣa], mother of gathering. So the two distinguished lexicographers Giauhari and Alcamus expressly write, and, among the writers on nature, Damir, often cited by us. Here is a striking example of this hen's φιλοστοργία [philostorgia] from Alpheus of Mytilene, Anthology book 1, ch. 87.

Χειμερίαις νιφάδεσσι παλυνομένα τιθὰς ὄρνις Τέκνοις εὐναίας ἀμφέχεε πτέρυγας· Μέσφά μιν οὐράνιον κρύος ὤλεσεν. ἦ γὰρ ἔμεινεν Αἰθέρος οὐρανίων ἀντίπαλος νεφέων. Πρόκνη, καὶ Μήδεια, κατ᾽ ἀΐδος αἰδέσθητε, Μητέρες, ὀρνιθίων ἔργα διδασκόμεναι. [Cheimeriais niphadessi palynomena tithas ornis teknois eunaias amphechee pterygas; mespha min ouranion kryos ōlesen. ē gar emeinen aitheros ouraniōn antipalos nepheōn. Proknē, kai Mēdeia, kat᾽ aidos aidesthēte, mēteres, ornithiōn erga didaskomenai.]
